A minaret is a tall, slender tower built as part of a mosque — the Islamic place of worship — from which Muslims are called to prayer.

Picture a very tall, narrow tower rising up from the ground — much taller than it is wide, almost like a giant pencil pointing toward the sky. It is typically cylindrical (round like a tube), though some are square or octagonal. Near the top, there is usually a small balcony that wraps around the tower. Above the balcony, the tower tapers into a pointed tip, often crowned with a crescent moon symbol, which is a widely recognized symbol of Islam.

The tower's surface is often beautifully decorated with geometric patterns, carved stonework, or tiles, depending on the region and era in which it was built.

The minaret's main purpose is functional: it serves as the platform from which the call to prayer — known as the adhan — is announced five times a day.

Islam requires its followers to pray five times daily, at specific times from dawn to night. Someone needed to let the community know when each prayer time had arrived. Traditionally, a man called the muezzin would climb the spiral staircase inside the minaret, step out onto the balcony, and call out the adhan in a loud, melodic voice so that people across the neighborhood could hear it and prepare for prayer.

Because the minaret is tall, the muezzin's voice could carry much farther than if he had simply stood at ground level. It worked as a natural amplifier of sound across the city.

In the modern world, most minarets no longer require the muezzin to physically climb them. Instead, loudspeakers are mounted on the balcony, and the adhan is broadcast electronically — sometimes even as a recording. But the tower itself remains.

Minarets are found wherever mosques are built. That means you will encounter them primarily in Muslim-majority countries — across the Middle East, North Africa, Central Asia, South Asia (including India and Pakistan), and Southeast Asia. However, because Muslim communities exist all over the world, minarets can be found on every continent, including in Europe and the Americas.

They are one of the most recognizable features of a city's skyline in the Islamic world. In places like Istanbul (Turkey), Cairo (Egypt), or Lahore (Pakistan), the skyline is famously dotted with the silhouettes of dozens of minarets rising above the rooftops.
How many minarets does a mosque have?

A mosque can have just one minaret or several. The number often signals the size, age, or prestige of the mosque:

  • A small neighborhood mosque might have just one.
  • A grand or historically important mosque might have two, four, or even six.
  • The famous Blue Mosque in Istanbul, for example, has six minarets — an extraordinary number that was considered highly unusual and even controversial when it was built in the early 1600s, because six minarets had previously been reserved only for the mosque in Mecca.

Over centuries, the minaret has grown beyond its practical role. It is now also a visual and cultural symbol — a marker in the landscape that says: there is a mosque here; this is a Muslim community. Much like a church steeple or a temple spire, the minaret announces the presence of religious life.

In that sense, it carries both architectural and spiritual weight. It reaches upward, which many interpret as a physical gesture toward the divine.
How to use the word in a sentence

• "The city's oldest mosque had a single minaret that had stood for eight hundred years."
  • "From the minaret, the muezzin's voice drifted across the town every morning at dawn."
  • "The architect designed a modern minaret that blended traditional form with contemporary materials."
  • "Travelers often describe the minarets of Istanbul as one of the most beautiful sights in the world."

A minaret is the tall, slender tower of a mosque, built so that the call to prayer can be sounded from its balcony and heard across the surrounding area — and which has also become one of the most enduring symbols of Islamic architecture and identity worldwide.
